screens.title: Introduction to C# Scripting in Unity
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we open the door from static scenes to interactive play by using C# in Unity. C# is the language you use to tell GameObjects how to behave: when to move, how to respond to input, and what to print to the Console so you can understand execution flow. You will learn the concrete steps to create a script file, ensure its filename matches the class name, attach it as a component to a GameObject, and use the MonoBehaviour lifecycle methods Awake, Start, Update and FixedUpdate to control initialization and frame or physics-driven updates. We’ll also look at simple variable declarations, how public variables expose parameters in the Inspector for rapid iteration, and the practical debugging habit of using Debug. Log to inspect runtime values. A small code example shows movement and logging so you can immediately see the connection between code and scene behavior. By the end of the module, you’ll be able to create a script, attach it, run it, and reason about when your code runs and why. Think about one simple behaviour you want to add to a cube or character; this chapter makes that idea tangible.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Introduction to C# Scripting
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Introduction to C# Scripting

Use C# to give behavior to GameObjects. Learn creation, lifecycle, variables, and debugging for immediate playtesting feedback.

GameObject
+ Script → Component
In this lesson
Create scripts, attach to objects, and run the SimpleMovement example to see code drive motion.
Core methods
Awake, Start, Update, FixedUpdate lifecycle and why each matters for initialization and physics.
Quick activity
Build a Bouncing Cube and use Debug.Log to inspect runtime values when you press Space.
Explore Key Topics
Scripts & Files
Name scripts to match the class so Unity compiles and lets you attach them.
Lifecycle
Use Awake for early setup, Start for first-frame setup, Update for per-frame logic.
Debugging
Debug.Log prints to Console so you can verify values and execution order.
Preview Snippet
public class SimpleMovement : MonoBehaviour
{
  public float moveSpeed = 5.0f;

  void Start()
  {
    transform.position = new Vector3(0, 1, 0);
  }

  void Update()
  {
    transform.Translate(Vector3.forward * moveSpeed * Time.deltaTime);
  }
}
Try creating a script named PlayerController and attach it to a Cube. This is where you begin iterating on gameplay.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus on practical skills you will use immediately when scripting in Unity. First, you will understand the role of C# and how it connects to GameObjects and Components. That matters because scripting is the mechanism that turns visual assets into interactive systems. Second, you will create, name, and attach C# scripts in the Unity editor and open them in your code editor. This objective includes the important convention that filenames match class names so Unity compiles correctly. Third, you will identify and use the key MonoBehaviour lifecycle methods: Awake, Start, Update and FixedUpdate. Knowing when each method runs prevents timing bugs and ensures reliable initialization and physics behavior. Fourth, you will declare variables of common types, expose public fields to the Inspector for quick tuning, and use Debug. Log to inspect runtime behavior. Each objective includes a practical example you can try immediately, such as creating a PlayerController script, toggling a public float from the Inspector, and printing position values to the Console. Together these skills let you build and iterate on simple game behaviours quickly and confidently.

screens.title: Bloom Progression
screens.narratorSegment: We scaffold learning from simple recognition to applied control. You will first learn to identify where scripts live and how filenames and class names must match. Then you will understand lifecycle ordering and how Awake and Start differ — especially when one script needs to provide a value before another script’s Start runs. Next, you apply that understanding to write movement or bouncing behaviours using Update or FixedUpdate and time-based movement so motion is frame-rate independent. Finally, you master debugging with Debug. Log and Inspector-driven tuning so you can iterate without recompiling every small change. Practically, this means you’ll be able to create a BouncingCube that exposes height and speed in the Inspector, observe its motion in Play mode, and print positions to the Console on user input to verify correctness. A common misconception is thinking Start runs before Awake; we’ll make that timing clear with examples so you avoid initialization order bugs. These progressive objectives get you from reading example scripts to iterating on your own game behaviours.

screens.title: Creating and Naming C# Scripts
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a new C# script in Unity is a small set of precise steps that prevents common compile-time headaches. In the Project window you use Create > C# Script, then give the file a meaningful name such as PlayerController or EnemyAI. The crucial rule is that the file name must match the public class name inside the file. Unity’s compiler links the filename to the declared class; mismatches produce compile errors or prevent the script from appearing as a component. After creating the file, double-click it to open in your code editor. Save after edits so Unity detects the change and recompiles. A common beginner mistake is renaming the file in the editor but not updating the class declaration, or vice versa. That leads to errors that look like the script can’t be attached. Another mistake is leaving unused using statements — they won’t break compilation, but they clutter the file. Practice: create a script named PlayerController, ensure the first line declares public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour, save, and then attach it to a GameObject. This habit keeps the link between file and class consistent and avoids wasting time diagnosing phantom issues.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Creating and Naming Scripts
Process

Create → Name → Save

  1. Create a new C# Script in the Project window via Create > C# Script.
  2. Name the script meaningfully, e.g. PlayerController or BouncingCube.
  3. Open in your code editor and ensure the public class name matches the filename exactly.
  4. Save the file so Unity recompiles and the script becomes attachable.
Common mistake
Renaming only the file or only the class; this causes compile errors and prevents attachment.
Pro tip
Use your editor's refactor->rename to change both at once, and save immediately so Unity recompiles.
Code Template
using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour
{
    void Start()
    {
        // Initialization
    }

    void Update()
    {
        // Per-frame logic
    }
}
Try This
Create PlayerController.cs, open it, confirm the class name, save, and attach it to a Cube.
Why It Matters
File-class mismatches are the single most common early frustration; fixing this speeds iteration.

screens.title: Attach and Manage Scripts on GameObjects
screens.narratorSegment: Attaching a script makes its code run for a specific GameObject. You can attach a script by dragging it from the Project window onto a GameObject in the Hierarchy or into the Inspector as a new component. A GameObject can host many scripts, which compose behaviour modularly — for example, one script can handle movement while another handles health. Likewise, the same script asset can be attached to many GameObjects to reuse behaviour. Watch for one frequent source of confusion: if your script is not visible in the Inspector after compilation, either compilation failed or the class and file names don’t match. Always check the Console for compile errors. Also confirm that the script component is enabled; a disabled component won’t receive Update calls. When testing, prefer small focused components that do one job; debugging becomes easier if you isolate responsibilities. Practice by creating a BouncingCube script, attach it to a Cube, and then duplicate the Cube to see the same behaviour applied to multiple objects without extra code changes. That exemplifies Unity’s component-based design and reduces duplicated logic. Attach and Manage Scripts on GameObjects means attach multiple small scripts to a gameobject to combine behaviours and reuse script assets across many objects.. In practical terms, how components compose behaviour and common attachment pitfalls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Attach & Manage
How to attach
  • Drag the script asset onto a GameObject in the Hierarchy.
  • Or select the GameObject and click Add Component, then choose the script.
  • Confirm the component appears and is enabled in the Inspector.
Manage components
Use multiple focused scripts rather than one large monolithic script. Reuse the same script asset across many objects for consistent behavior.
Common issue: Component missing because of a compile error or a filename/class mismatch. Check the Console first.
Example
Single Cube
Attach BouncingCube to one Cube to give it vertical motion and Console logging on Space.
Multiple Cubes
Duplicate the Cube to reuse the same BouncingCube script without adding code.
Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

Attaching scripts as components composes behaviour and enables reuse; verify compilation and naming if the component does not appear.

screens.title: MonoBehaviour and Lifecycle Methods
screens.narratorSegment: MonoBehaviour is the base class for scripts that interact with Unity’s engine and scene objects. When your class inherits from MonoBehaviour, Unity can call special lifecycle methods at predictable times. Awake is called when the script instance is loaded and is the earliest place to initialize internal data or grab references to components on the same GameObject. Start runs on the first frame that the script is enabled, and it is suitable for setting initial game state that might depend on other objects' Awake methods having already run. Update is called once per frame and is the place for input checks, per-frame movement, and non-physics logic. For physics updates that must be consistent across variable frame rates, FixedUpdate runs at a fixed timestep and is the preferred place for applying forces to a Rigidbody. A common misconception is to put physics code in Update; that can create inconsistent behavior because Update’s timing depends on frame rate. Concrete example: store an initial Y position in Start, then use Update to animate position using Time. deltaTime, or use FixedUpdate to apply Rigidbody forces. Reflect: which initialization could another script rely on — Awake or Start?

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle Purpose
keyIdea.text: Use Awake for earliest initialization, Start for first-frame state, Update for frame-based logic, and FixedUpdate for stable physics operations.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › MonoBehaviour & Lifecycle
Definition

What MonoBehaviour gives you

  • Automatic method calls at defined moments (Awake, Start, Update, FixedUpdate).
  • Access to Unity API like transform, GetComponent, and Time.deltaTime.
  • Ability to be added as a component to GameObjects in the Inspector.
Quick reference
Awake() — earliest initialization
Start() — first enabled frame
Update() — per-frame work
FixedUpdate() — physics timestep
Example & Misconception
Example: Use Awake to cache a Rigidbody reference using GetComponent<Rigidbody>(). Use Start to set the initial position. If you apply AddForce to a Rigidbody, do so in FixedUpdate to avoid varying results across different frame rates.
Misconception
Putting physics AddForce calls in Update will yield inconsistent physics because Update timing varies with frame rate.
Check your understanding
If Script A must provide data for Script B’s Start, which lifecycle method should Script A use to guarantee early initialization? Consider Awake vs Start.

screens.title: Awake vs Start — Initialization Order
screens.narratorSegment: Awake and Start both run before your first gameplay frame, but they serve slightly different purposes and are called at different times. Awake runs when the script instance is loaded, which happens even if the component is initially disabled. Use Awake to initialize internal variables and to get references to components on the same GameObject, for example storing a Rigidbody or Animator reference with GetComponent. Start runs on the first frame the script is enabled, which gives a small but important ordering guarantee relative to other objects' Awake calls. If another script needs a value from your script in its Start, initialize that value in Awake so it’s available early. A practical example from the assessment: to initialize playerCount to zero before other scripts read it in Start, set playerCount in Awake. A common mistake is assuming Start always fires before any other Start; while Start runs before the first Update, Awake executes earlier during the load phase. Closing question: when might you intentionally delay initialization to Start rather than Awake, and what could depend on that decision? Awake vs Start — Initialization Order means use awake for earliest guaranteed initialization, and start for setup that can wait until the object is enabled for the first frame.. In practical terms, when to use awake and when start is more appropriate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Awake vs Start
Awake
Runs when the script instance is loaded. Ideal for caching references and performing initialization that must exist before any other object's Start runs.
Example
Set playerCount = 0 in Awake so other scripts reading that value in Start see the correct initial value.
Start
Runs on the first frame the script is enabled. Use for state that depends on other objects having completed their Awake logic.
Example
Set the initial position or UI values that may depend on other objects’ Awake setup.
Misconception check
Do not assume both run at the same time. Awake always executes earlier in the loading sequence than Start; if timing matters, prefer Awake for earliest initialization.

screens.title: Update vs FixedUpdate — Frame vs Physics Timing
screens.narratorSegment: Update and FixedUpdate are both repeating methods, but they serve different timing needs. Update is called every frame and its frequency depends on the frame rate. Use Update for non-physics tasks such as reading player input, performing interpolation, or manipulating transforms directly for simple motion. Because frame rates vary, apply Time. deltaTime to your movement calculations so motion remains consistent across machines. FixedUpdate, by contrast, runs at a fixed timestep configured in the Physics settings and should be used for physics operations like applying forces to a Rigidbody. This separation ensures consistent physics simulations independent of render performance. A common novice error is applying AddForce inside Update; the result can feel jittery or vary across systems. Concrete example: if you want to move a Rigidbody forward reliably, call rb. AddForce in FixedUpdate; if you want to move a non-Rigidbody transform smoothly, use transform. Translate with Time. deltaTime inside Update. Final check: if motion is physics-driven, prefer FixedUpdate; otherwise Update with delta-time is acceptable for simple, frame-based motion. Update vs FixedUpdate — Frame vs Physics Timing means use update for per-frame input and transform tweaks with time.deltatime and fixedupdate for consistent physics operations on rigidbodies.. In practical terms, choosing the right per-frame or fixed-timestep method. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Update vs FixedUpdate
Update
Frame-dependent. Use for input, animations, and transform changes. Apply Time.deltaTime to keep movement frame-rate independent.
Code hint
// Move forward smoothly
transform.Translate(Vector3.forward * moveSpeed * Time.deltaTime);
FixedUpdate
Fixed timestep. Use for applying forces or other Rigidbody-based physics so simulation remains consistent.
Code hint
// Apply physics force in FixedUpdate
rb.AddForce(Vector3.up * jumpStrength);
Example Scenario
You have a player that should move responsively when a key is pressed and also be affected by gravity. Read input in Update and apply physics-based movement in FixedUpdate to keep responsiveness and stable collisions.

screens.title: Variables, Types, and Inspector Exposure
screens.narratorSegment: Variables store the data your scripts need. In C# you declare variables by naming a data type, then the variable name. Common types include int for whole numbers, float for decimals, string for text, bool for true or false values, and Vector3 for positions or directions in 3D space. Public variables are exposed in the Inspector — for example public float moveSpeed = 5.0f — letting you tune values from the Editor without changing code. Remember to append an f to float literals, like 5.0f, so C# treats them as floats. Private variables are internal to the script and invisible in the Inspector. Use public fields for parameters that designers or you will tweak frequently and private fields for internal counters or state. Misconception: making everything public is not a good long-term strategy; expose only what you need to tweak, and keep internal state private. Concrete example: declare public float bounceHeight and public float bounceSpeed for the BouncingCube so you can adjust height and speed during playtesting. These small habits speed iteration and keep the Inspector useful for tuning gameplay.

keyIdea.title: Expose only what you tune
keyIdea.text: Use public fields to make tweakable parameters editable in the Inspector, but keep internal state private to avoid accidental edits.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Variables & Inspector
Types
  • int — whole numbers
  • float — decimals; use 5.0f suffix
  • string — text
  • bool — true/false
  • Vector3 — 3D position or direction
Public vs Private
Public fields show in the Inspector for quick tuning; private fields keep implementation details hidden. Use public for parameters and private for state like counters.
Example
public float bounceHeight = 1.0f;
public float bounceSpeed = 2.0f;

private float originalY; // internal state, not shown in Inspector
Try
Change bounceHeight in the Inspector while the game is running to see instant effects without recompiling.
Why private?
Keep counters and runtime state private so designers don't accidentally change them from the Inspector.

screens.title: Debug.Log — Observing Runtime Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: Debug. Log is the simplest and most immediate way to inspect what your script does while the game runs. You can print small messages, variable values, or object references to Unity’s Console window. Use it to confirm that Awake or Start has executed, to verify inputs are read correctly, or to check position values at a key moment. For example, Debug. Log("Bouncing Cube Initialized!") in Start tells you the script started successfully. You can also combine strings and variables, for instance Debug. Log("Current health: " + currentHealth), to observe changing state. Be careful not to log heavy messages every frame in Update without gating them, because frequent logging can slow down the Editor and flood the Console. A practical tip is to log conditionally, such as when the Space key is pressed, or only when a threshold is crossed. Use Debug. LogWarning and Debug. LogError for higher-severity messages. After debugging, remove or guard frequent logs to keep performance healthy. Question to ponder: what value would you log to confirm a movement calculation is using Time. deltaTime correctly? Debug.Log — Observing Runtime Behavior means log key events and conditional values to verify execution without overwhelming the console or harming performance.. In practical terms, using console output to verify code execution and variable values. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › SimpleMovement Walkthrough
Full example
using UnityEngine; // Essential for Unity-specific classes like MonoBehaviour, Vector3, etc.

public class SimpleMovement : MonoBehaviour
{
    // Public variable, editable in the Unity Inspector
    public float moveSpeed = 5.0f;

    // Private variable, not directly editable in the Inspector
    private int score = 0;

    // Awake is called when the script instance is being loaded
    void Awake()
    {
        Debug.Log("SimpleMovement script has Woken Up!");
    }

    // Start is called before the first frame update
    void Start()
    {
        Debug.Log("SimpleMovement script has Started!");
        transform.position = new Vector3(0, 1, 0);
    }

    // Update is called once per frame
    void Update()
    {
        transform.Translate(Vector3.forward * moveSpeed * Time.deltaTime);

        if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.S))
        {
            score += 10;
            Debug.Log("Score: " + score);
        }
    }

    // FixedUpdate is called at a fixed interval, ideal for physics operations
    void FixedUpdate()
    {
        // Physics code would go here
    }
}
What to watch
Observe Console logs for Awake and Start to confirm order.
Runtime tweak
Adjust moveSpeed in the Inspector during Play to see immediate effect.
Misconception
Logging every frame is fine for short tests but can slow the Editor if left enabled long-term.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Bouncing Cube Activity
Steps
  1. Create a Cube at (0, 0.5, 0).
  2. Create BouncingCube.cs and attach to the Cube.
  3. Declare public float bounceHeight and bounceSpeed; store originalY in Start.
  4. In Update set newY = originalY + Mathf.Sin(Time.time * bounceSpeed) * bounceHeight and assign transform.position.
  5. Add Debug.Log in Start and conditional Debug.Log on Space in Update.
Test
Run Play, watch the Cube bounce, press Space to see current Y in the Console, and tweak bounceHeight and bounceSpeed in the Inspector.
Starter Code
using UnityEngine;

public class BouncingCube : MonoBehaviour
{
    public float bounceHeight = 1.0f;
    public float bounceSpeed = 2.0f;

    private float originalY;

    void Start()
    {
        Debug.Log("Bouncing Cube Initialized!");
        originalY = transform.position.y;
    }

    void Update()
    {
        float newY = originalY + (Mathf.Sin(Time.time * bounceSpeed) * bounceHeight);
        transform.position = new Vector3(transform.position.x, newY, transform.position.z);

        if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space))
        {
            Debug.Log("Current Cube Y Position: " + transform.position.y);
        }
    }
}
Adjust the public fields in Play mode to iterate without recompiling. This is the fastest loop for small gameplay tweaks.

screens.title: Saving, GetComponent and transform Usage
screens.narratorSegment: Small habits make development smoother. Always save your script files after editing; Unity recompiles only saved files and unsaved edits are a common source of confusion. Use GetComponent to cache references in Awake or Start so you avoid repeated costly lookups. For example, store a Rigidbody reference in a private field with myRigidbody = GetComponent<Rigidbody>() in Awake. Use transform property for simple position and rotation changes when you don't require physics; transform is a built-in shorthand on MonoBehaviour. However, if you are manipulating a Rigidbody, prefer its A P I to keep physics consistent. Keep scripts focused: one responsibility per component makes debugging and reuse easier. Keep public fields limited to parameters you tune and keep runtime counters private. Finally, after testing, remove noisy Console logs or gate them behind input checks to prevent performance issues. These small practices reduce compile errors, improve runtime performance, and make it faster to iterate on gameplay features like movement or bouncing behaviours. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we open the door from static scenes to interactive play by using C# in Unity. C# is the language you use to tell GameObjects how to behave: when to move, how to respond to input, and what to print to the Console so you can understand execution flow. You will learn the concrete steps to create a script file, ensure its filename matches the class name, attach it as a component to a GameObject, and use the MonoBehaviour lifecycle methods Awake, Start, Update and FixedUpdate to control initialization and frame or physics-driven updates. We’ll also look at simple variable declarations, how public variables expose parameters in the Inspector for rapid iteration, and the practical debugging habit of using Debug. Log to inspect runtime values. A small code example shows movement and logging so you can immediately see the connection between code and scene behavior. By the end of the module, you’ll be able to create a script, attach it, run it, and reason about when your code runs and why. Think about one simple behaviour you want to add to a cube or character; this chapter makes that idea tangible.

These objectives focus on practical skills you will use immediately when scripting in Unity. First, you will understand the role of C# and how it connects to GameObjects and Components. That matters because scripting is the mechanism that turns visual assets into interactive systems. Second, you will create, name, and attach C# scripts in the Unity editor and open them in your code editor. This objective includes the important convention that filenames match class names so Unity compiles correctly. Third, you will identify and use the key MonoBehaviour lifecycle methods: Awake, Start, Update and FixedUpdate. Knowing when each method runs prevents timing bugs and ensures reliable initialization and physics behavior. Fourth, you will declare variables of common types, expose public fields to the Inspector for quick tuning, and use Debug. Log to inspect runtime behavior. Each objective includes a practical example you can try immediately, such as creating a PlayerController script, toggling a public float from the Inspector, and printing position values to the Console. Together these skills let you build and iterate on simple game behaviours quickly and confidently.

We scaffold learning from simple recognition to applied control. You will first learn to identify where scripts live and how filenames and class names must match. Then you will understand lifecycle ordering and how Awake and Start differ — especially when one script needs to provide a value before another script’s Start runs. Next, you apply that understanding to write movement or bouncing behaviours using Update or FixedUpdate and time-based movement so motion is frame-rate independent. Finally, you master debugging with Debug. Log and Inspector-driven tuning so you can iterate without recompiling every small change. Practically, this means you’ll be able to create a BouncingCube that exposes height and speed in the Inspector, observe its motion in Play mode, and print positions to the Console on user input to verify correctness. A common misconception is thinking Start runs before Awake; we’ll make that timing clear with examples so you avoid initialization order bugs. These progressive objectives get you from reading example scripts to iterating on your own game behaviours.

Creating a new C# script in Unity is a small set of precise steps that prevents common compile-time headaches. In the Project window you use Create > C# Script, then give the file a meaningful name such as PlayerController or EnemyAI. The crucial rule is that the file name must match the public class name inside the file. Unity’s compiler links the filename to the declared class; mismatches produce compile errors or prevent the script from appearing as a component. After creating the file, double-click it to open in your code editor. Save after edits so Unity detects the change and recompiles. A common beginner mistake is renaming the file in the editor but not updating the class declaration, or vice versa. That leads to errors that look like the script can’t be attached. Another mistake is leaving unused using statements — they won’t break compilation, but they clutter the file. Practice: create a script named PlayerController, ensure the first line declares public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour, save, and then attach it to a GameObject. This habit keeps the link between file and class consistent and avoids wasting time diagnosing phantom issues.

Attaching a script makes its code run for a specific GameObject. You can attach a script by dragging it from the Project window onto a GameObject in the Hierarchy or into the Inspector as a new component. A GameObject can host many scripts, which compose behaviour modularly — for example, one script can handle movement while another handles health. Likewise, the same script asset can be attached to many GameObjects to reuse behaviour. Watch for one frequent source of confusion: if your script is not visible in the Inspector after compilation, either compilation failed or the class and file names don’t match. Always check the Console for compile errors. Also confirm that the script component is enabled; a disabled component won’t receive Update calls. When testing, prefer small focused components that do one job; debugging becomes easier if you isolate responsibilities. Practice by creating a BouncingCube script, attach it to a Cube, and then duplicate the Cube to see the same behaviour applied to multiple objects without extra code changes. That exemplifies Unity’s component-based design and reduces duplicated logic. Attach and Manage Scripts on GameObjects means attach multiple small scripts to a gameobject to combine behaviours and reuse script assets across many objects.. In practical terms, how components compose behaviour and common attachment pitfalls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

MonoBehaviour is the base class for scripts that interact with Unity’s engine and scene objects. When your class inherits from MonoBehaviour, Unity can call special lifecycle methods at predictable times. Awake is called when the script instance is loaded and is the earliest place to initialize internal data or grab references to components on the same GameObject. Start runs on the first frame that the script is enabled, and it is suitable for setting initial game state that might depend on other objects' Awake methods having already run. Update is called once per frame and is the place for input checks, per-frame movement, and non-physics logic. For physics updates that must be consistent across variable frame rates, FixedUpdate runs at a fixed timestep and is the preferred place for applying forces to a Rigidbody. A common misconception is to put physics code in Update; that can create inconsistent behavior because Update’s timing depends on frame rate. Concrete example: store an initial Y position in Start, then use Update to animate position using Time. deltaTime, or use FixedUpdate to apply Rigidbody forces. Reflect: which initialization could another script rely on — Awake or Start?

Awake and Start both run before your first gameplay frame, but they serve slightly different purposes and are called at different times. Awake runs when the script instance is loaded, which happens even if the component is initially disabled. Use Awake to initialize internal variables and to get references to components on the same GameObject, for example storing a Rigidbody or Animator reference with GetComponent. Start runs on the first frame the script is enabled, which gives a small but important ordering guarantee relative to other objects' Awake calls. If another script needs a value from your script in its Start, initialize that value in Awake so it’s available early. A practical example from the assessment: to initialize playerCount to zero before other scripts read it in Start, set playerCount in Awake. A common mistake is assuming Start always fires before any other Start; while Start runs before the first Update, Awake executes earlier during the load phase. Closing question: when might you intentionally delay initialization to Start rather than Awake, and what could depend on that decision? Awake vs Start — Initialization Order means use awake for earliest guaranteed initialization, and start for setup that can wait until the object is enabled for the first frame.. In practical terms, when to use awake and when start is more appropriate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Update and FixedUpdate are both repeating methods, but they serve different timing needs. Update is called every frame and its frequency depends on the frame rate. Use Update for non-physics tasks such as reading player input, performing interpolation, or manipulating transforms directly for simple motion. Because frame rates vary, apply Time. deltaTime to your movement calculations so motion remains consistent across machines. FixedUpdate, by contrast, runs at a fixed timestep configured in the Physics settings and should be used for physics operations like applying forces to a Rigidbody. This separation ensures consistent physics simulations independent of render performance. A common novice error is applying AddForce inside Update; the result can feel jittery or vary across systems. Concrete example: if you want to move a Rigidbody forward reliably, call rb. AddForce in FixedUpdate; if you want to move a non-Rigidbody transform smoothly, use transform. Translate with Time. deltaTime inside Update. Final check: if motion is physics-driven, prefer FixedUpdate; otherwise Update with delta-time is acceptable for simple, frame-based motion. Update vs FixedUpdate — Frame vs Physics Timing means use update for per-frame input and transform tweaks with time.deltatime and fixedupdate for consistent physics operations on rigidbodies.. In practical terms, choosing the right per-frame or fixed-timestep method. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Variables store the data your scripts need. In C# you declare variables by naming a data type, then the variable name. Common types include int for whole numbers, float for decimals, string for text, bool for true or false values, and Vector3 for positions or directions in 3D space. Public variables are exposed in the Inspector — for example public float moveSpeed = 5.0f — letting you tune values from the Editor without changing code. Remember to append an f to float literals, like 5.0f, so C# treats them as floats. Private variables are internal to the script and invisible in the Inspector. Use public fields for parameters that designers or you will tweak frequently and private fields for internal counters or state. Misconception: making everything public is not a good long-term strategy; expose only what you need to tweak, and keep internal state private.
